title: Release, handover and no-certification claims
audience: Cleaners and supervisors completing industrial degreasing handover.
learningOutcomes: Describe what a cleaner's handover covers, and what it does not.
Refuse a request to certify plant or chemical safety.
Record exclusions and restricted work in a handover that the owner can verify.

instruction.heading: What a cleaner's handover covers
instruction.body: A cleaner's handover is a factual account of the housekeeping and inspection work that was carried out, with the areas, the methods and the products named. It lists what was cleaned, what was looked at, what was seen, and how it was checked. It lists the exclusions, which are the parts of the job that were not done, could not be reached or were removed from scope. It lists the restricted work that remains open, and it names the person who holds each open decision. Above all, it says what the handover is not. It does not describe the plant as safe to operate, the chemicals as cleared for disposal or reuse, or the area as released for production or restart. Those are decisions for the owner and the competent person, and they are made on evidence that the cleaner's handover does not provide.

instruction.heading: Why a cleaning completion is not a certificate
instruction.body: A completed clean is a record of work, not a statement about the safety of the plant. A cleaner who has wiped a machine has not tested its isolation, verified its controls, assessed its chemicals or checked its guarding. The handover should make that distinction plain. Where a document is presented to a customer or the owner as a statement about the safety, condition or compliance of a plant or product, it is a representation the business is making. The ACCC's page on false or misleading claims (dated 28 June 2026) treats such statements as needing accuracy, reasonable grounds and evidence behind them, and it does not treat the speaker's intention as the test. A cleaner should not sign a document that says the plant is safe or the chemicals are cleared when the cleaner has no evidence of those things.

instruction.heading: Refusing a certificate and referring it
instruction.body: If someone asks you to sign a certificate that a plant or chemical is safe, or that a degreasing area may restart, refuse. Keep the refusal calm and factual. You might explain that your handover covers the cleaning and inspection you performed, that it does not cover the isolation, the controls or the chemical assessment, and that the decision belongs to the competent person. Refer the request in writing to the person who holds that decision, and name the document you were asked to sign. Record the request, the requester, the time, the document, your response and the referral. Do not offer a softer version of the certificate, such as one that says the work was 'done to a safe standard', because that phrasing still describes safety and is not supported by your evidence.

instruction.heading: Exclusions and restricted work
instruction.body: List exclusions and restricted work plainly so that the next person knows what remains open. Every area not cleaned should be named, with the reason it was not done. Every item not inspected should be listed, along with what stopped the inspection, such as access, an active isolation or a missing permit. Restricted work should be described in terms of what cannot be done until someone else decides, and who that person is. A handover that hides an exclusion is a false record, even if each line in it is accurate, because the reader will assume the work is complete. If the owner asks you to remove an exclusion from the handover to make it look finished, refuse and record the request. The exclusion stays in the record until the owner, in writing, confirms it has been resolved.

instruction.heading: A handover the owner can check
instruction.body: A handover the owner can check has an evidence index that points to where each supporting record is kept, a date and time on each entry, the names of the people who did each part, and the signature of both the person who performed the work and the person who received the handover. Corrections are made with a single line through the error, initials, a date and a reason, so that the original is still readable. Records are not replaced, backfilled or rewritten after the event. If a record is missing, state that in the handover and explain what has been done to find it. Photographs are taken only where the site procedure and the owner permit them, and they should show the condition without moving anything. The owner should be able to read the handover and decide, on the evidence, what is still to be done.

instruction.heading: Restart and release belong to someone else
instruction.body: Release for restart and clearance for chemical use are decisions made by the owner and the competent person, after they have checked the plant, the isolation, the guarding, the controls and the chemical assessment. The Safe Work Australia guidance on managing WHS risks makes clear that a duty holder keeps its obligations when it passes work on, and warns against presuming that another party has a matter covered. For a cleaner, this means the handover supports the owner's decision and does not replace it. Once the handover is signed, the restart decision still needs its own record, made by the person who holds it. The cleaner should not be asked to make that decision, and should refuse to be drawn into making it in the course of a handover conversation.

procedure: Describe the housekeeping done and the inspection performed, using the zone names and methods the site uses, without safety or clearance claims.
List every exclusion, with the reason it was not done, and every restricted item, with the person who holds the decision.
Refuse any request to certify plant or chemical safety, or to state that an area may restart, and refer the request in writing.
Do not remove or soften an exclusion or restricted item at the owner's request without written confirmation that it has been resolved.
Check that the evidence index points to every supporting record, and that every entry is dated and signed.
Correct any error with a single line, initials, date and reason, and do not replace or backfill any record.
Record the request, the response, the people informed and the handover status, and complete the handover only when the owner has confirmed the restricted items in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A supervisor asks you to sign a certificate that the degreasing area is safe to restart. You have cleaned the outside of the machine and wiped the guards, but you did not check the isolation. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you sign, and what do you say?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse to sign the certificate. Explain that the handover covers the cleaning and inspection you carried out, that you did not check the isolation or the controls, and that the restart decision belongs to the competent person. Refer the request to the competent person in writing, and record the request, your response and the referral. Do not offer a reworded certificate that still says the area is safe.

workedExamples.situation: You could not get access to the inside of a tank because the access permit was not issued. Your draft handover lists the tank as cleaned, because the owner says it was 'probably done last month'. (Example scenario.)
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How does the handover describe the tank?
workedExamples.reasoning: List the tank as an exclusion. Record that access was not available because the permit was not issued, and that the interior was not cleaned or inspected by you. Do not accept last month's clean as this job's clean, and do not describe the tank as cleaned. Name the owner as the person who decides whether the tank is to be entered and by whom. Keep the exclusion until the owner confirms it in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A customer asks for a letter that states the degreasing chemicals have been cleared for disposal, so that the customer can sell the waste on. (Example scenario; the customer and the chemicals are fictional.)
workedExamples.reasoning: No. A letter that clears chemicals for disposal or resale is a statement about a product that you cannot substantiate. Refuse the letter. Offer a factual record of the work done and the evidence held, and refer the request to the owner and the lawful waste contractor. Record the request, your response and the referral.

equipmentAndPpe: Handover record form with sections for work done, inspections, exclusions, restricted work and decision owners.
Evidence index listing where each supporting record is kept and for how long.
Refusal and referral form for certificate or clearance requests.
Site register of hazardous chemicals, to check which chemicals were in the area.
Pen or approved electronic record system with a correction method.
Gloves, eye protection and closed footwear as set by the SDS and the site procedure, where the handover involves a visit to the area.

commonErrors.error: Signing a certificate of plant safety or chemical clearance.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse, explain what the handover covers, and refer the decision to the competent person in writing.

commonErrors.error: Leaving exclusions out of the handover.
commonErrors.prevention: List every area and item not done or not reached, with the reason, and keep it until the owner confirms it is resolved.

commonErrors.error: Describing the area as cleared, released or safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe only the work done and the inspections made.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a previous clean as evidence for this job.
commonErrors.prevention: Record only what was done and seen on this job. Previous work is a separate matter for the owner.

commonErrors.error: Replacing or backfilling a record to make the handover look complete.
commonErrors.prevention: Correct errors with a single line, initials, date and reason. Record missing items as missing.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The ACCC's page on false or misleading claims (dated 28 June 2026) treats statements about a business's products or services as needing accuracy, reasonable grounds and evidence. A cleaner should not sign a statement about plant or chemical safety that the business cannot back up.

The Safe Work Australia register guidance (no publication date; the page shows 2011 as the model law date) describes a register of hazardous chemicals that is held at the workplace, kept up to date, and carries a current SDS for each listed chemical. Use the register to check which chemicals were in the area before listing them in the handover.

The Safe Work Australia guidance on managing WHS risks (How to manage WHS risks, December 2011, section 1.3) holds that a duty holder keeps its obligations when work is passed on, and asks parties to find out who is doing what rather than presume it.
This lesson does not state what those requirements are.
This lesson does not grant any licence, certificate, plant-safety approval, chemical clearance or fire-safety approval, and completing it does not make a cleaner a specialist or an inspector.

qualityStandard: Handover in the case study describes only the housekeeping and inspection performed, with no safety, release or clearance claims.
Certificate request in the case study is refused, the reason is given, and the request is referred in writing.
Every exclusion and restricted item is listed with its reason and the person who holds the decision.
No record in the exercise has been removed, softened or backfilled.
documentationEvidence: Handover record with work done, inspections, exclusions, restricted work and decision owners.
Refusal and referral record for the certificate or clearance request, with the referral recipient and date.
Evidence index showing where each supporting record is kept.
summary: A handover describes the work done, the inspections made, the exclusions and the restricted work.
A cleaning completion is not a certificate of plant or chemical safety; refuse such certificates and refer them.
List every exclusion, keep it until the owner confirms it in writing, and never backfill a record.

knowledgeChecks.question: Can a cleaner sign a certificate that a degreasing area is safe to restart?
options: Yes, after cleaning, since the area is now clean and dry
Yes, if the supervisor agrees, once the area is clean and dry
No, refuse and refer the restart decision to the competent person

knowledgeChecks.question: What must a handover list?
options: Only the price of the job and the amount charged to the client for the work
The work done, the inspections made, the exclusions and the restricted work
Only the cleaner's name, the date and the time of the visit to the site

knowledgeChecks.question: When can the handover be completed?
options: Immediately, once the cleaning is finished and the area is clean
When the shift ends and the crew has packed the kit away
When the owner has confirmed the outstanding decisions in writing
